title: Leading and Managing Remote Teams (including humanitarian specifics)
html:
In 2016, I was tasked with setting up a geographically-distributed digital team in UN-OCHA. Although I had been working remotely with people from around the world and managing a few individuals remotely over the previous decade, setting up a completely remote team was a new venture for me. I knew that it was possible yet recognized the biggest hurdle would be that I had to operate within a larger in-office organizational culture. (Yes, I had to commute to an office in order to telecommute with my team) As our team found our stride and we showed what was possible (e.g. higher quality services, more stable solutions), the in-office barrier became less of an issue. And, my focus began to shift towards how remote teams could be optimized while remaining highly productive.

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, I had started my own informal research reading about companies and digital humanitarian organizations that were entirely remote. I wanted a checklist to tell me (and management) what needed to be done. But, I recognized that a proper analysis would need to be undertaken before such a list could be built and customized for the traditional humanitarian sector.  With the outbreak of the pandemic, remote work quickly hit the mainstream. Leveraging that shift, I was able to convince Dijie (Sariel) Lei to join me to research the topic in 2021. 

The pandemic has really pushed remote work and remote teams to the forefront. We can no longer treat it as a fringe activity. The Harvard Business Review pointed out that, unfortunately, most organizations simply took their offices online during the pandemic, along with the bad habits that permeated them. Instead of back-to-back meetings, people got back-to-back Zoom calls. Instead of physical interruptions, they got more interruptions via Slack or Teams. Sadly, most managers or leaders were not ready for the shift. And, many continue to hold out hope for the office-first culture to return.

Yet, managers need to recognize that the world has changed. During a recent 60 Minutes interview, Karen Kimbrough of LinkedIn noted that 1-in-7 jobs advertised on their platform is now remote versus just 1-in-67 pre-pandemic. And, apparently Americans are now 2.5 times more likely to apply for a remote job than before. People are quitting their jobs in record numbers and looking for remote jobs with more flexibility. Some big companies are adjusting to the future and offering flexibility to help retain top talent. For example, Price Waterhouse Cooper recently offered thousands of employees full-time remote work.

So, how do we make sure that we optimally adjust to remote work? How do we attract and retain top talent? How do we keep our team operating at its peak, especially if responding to global-scale disasters? Leveraging a detailed literature review and interviews with real trail blazers in this subject, Sariel and I have put together Leading and Managing Remote Teams - Including Specifics for Disaster Response Teams. Rather than building something specific for my team or even UN-OCHA, we drafted it in a way that most any organization can easily consume and customize the content to their context thereby setting them on the path to better remote teams.

[PDF]

And, yes, the paper includes a checklist :)

Andrej
teaser: A practical paper with Sariel Lei on leading remote teams, built on the author's UN-OCHA experience, and including a checklist.
seo_description: Guidance on leading and managing remote teams, with humanitarian specifics, drawing on UN-OCHA's remote digital team and pandemic-era research.
